Challenges of tumour resection

Cancer is a life-threatening disease that is very difficult to treat because of the recurrence after surgical resection. Cancer surgeries are challenging because a ‘complete’ resection may risk damaging surrounding tissue and affecting organ function, whereas a safer and more cautious approach is often followed by tumour recurrence, so patients must undergo follow-up treatments like chemotherapy or second stage surgery (22). More fundamentally, tumour boundaries are often indistinguishable to the naked eye, and smaller lesions can easily remain obscured during surgery. These factors all contribute to the high recurrence rate of cancer.

  • Intraoperative scanning and subsequent image processing are time-consuming, so the guidance is technically not in real time, causing delay in surgery

​

  • Most images are qualitative, they are not linked to any absolute biochemical measurements, so the information provided from the images is limited.

rich.comp-mjqv61ry: Compared to normal cells, cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis rather than oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production despite the presence of oxygen, which is known as the Warburg effect (2), The Warburg effect is one of the phenomenon that shows cancer cells modify their metabolism to support proliferation. Although the Warburg effect was rationalised by benefits such as promoting ATP synthesis and biosynthesis, it does not fully explain the metabolism in cancer cell (3).
rich.comp-mjqw9lmj:
The Warburg effect is characterised by increased glycolytic flux and increased NAD+ demand, which is supported by mechanisms including malate-aspartate shuttle and lactate fermentation (4). Furthermore, adaptation of cancer cells also include shift in biosynthetic pathways and reactive oxygen species production (5), so both NADH and NADPH level are affected.


Moreira et al. found that the [NAD+]/[NADH] and [NADP+]/[NADPH] ratios are increased approximately fivefold and tenfold in cancer cells relative to normal cells (6). 

​

Potential Rationale:​​

  • In order to maintain high glycolytic rate in cancer cells, pyruvate needs to be rapidly removed, while NAD+ needs to be rapidly replenished. This is achieved by the expression of lactate dehydrogenase, which couples the reduction of pyruvate with the oxidation of NADH, resulting in a high [NAD+]/[NADH] ratio that maintains the glycolytic flux (7).

​

  • The high [NADP+]/[NADPH] ratio can be attributed to the increased use of NADPH as a reducing agent for generation of antioxidant defence and anabolic reactions such as nucleotide, amino acid and fatty acid synthesis (8).
rich.comp-mjqyrqwg: Distinguish cancer tissues from normal tissues
rich.comp-mjqyrqwj:
Although the Warburg effect is not a universal phenomenon for all cancer types, it has been shown consistently that the metabolism and microenvironment cancer cells is significantly different from normal cells. These affect the properties of fluorescence molecules.


Since NAD(P)H is intrinsically fluorescent (9), whereas its oxidised forms are not, fluorescence imaging allows the redox state to be assessed without using any exogenous fluorescence probes. Research has shown that brain tumour tissues emit lower autofluorescence intensity than normal tissues, so fluorescence imaging could allow delineation of tumour resection margin (10-12). However, the clinical application of this intensity-based approach is constrained by significant limitations:

​

  • Non-uniform illumination artefacts: The fluorescence image is bright at the centre, but intensity drops at the periphery due to uneven illumination of endoscope (12)

​

  • Low sensitivity: NAD(P)H has low quantum yield, so fluorescence image has low signal to noise ratio due to background fluorescence (13)

​

  • Haemoglobin absorption: fluorescence intensity signals are attenuated by haemoglobin, so blood vessels in tissue may affect discrimination between tumour and normal tissue (14)

rich.comp-mjr05q8h:
In contrast to fluorescence intensity measurements, fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) provides a robust metric for delineating tumour resection margin.

​

Fluorescence lifetime is the duration in which a fluorophore stays in its excited state before returning to the ground state. The fluorescence lifetime of a fluorophore is largely determined by the non-radiative decay rate, in other words, the restraint of molecular motion. For example, low temperature, high viscosity or a protein-bound state hinders non-radiative relaxation, thereby increases the fluorescence lifetime. Therefore, fluorescence lifetime is very sensitive to microenvironment and metabolic states.​

** Please check the Science for non-specialists page for the basics of FLIM

​

It has been demonstrated that FLIM enabled discrimination between glioblastoma and normal cortex with a high statistical significance (p = 0.0027), more robust than intensity-based imaging (p = 0.0199) (12).
rich.comp-mjra4ro8: Figure: Fluorescence lifetime image of normal cortex (left) and glioblastoma (right). (Sun et al., 2010)
rich.comp-mjraec6l:
The robustness of FLIM is largely attributed to the fact that fluorescence lifetime is an intrinsic property, independent of NAD(P)H concentration and the detected intensity (15). Therefore, fluorescence lifetime remains uniform across the field of view, unaffected by background lighting.

​

Furthermore, fluorescence lifetime is influenced by various parameters that differentiate tumour from normal tissues. For example, the free and protein-bound states of NAD(P)H have distinct fluorescence lifetimes, and the free to bound ratio of NADH is linked to [NAD+]/[NADH] ratio (16, 17). In addition, the fluorescence lifetime of enzyme-bound NADH and NADPH are different and the lifetimes depend on enzyme binding configuration and which enzyme NAD(P)H is bound (18, 19). Therefore, the metabolic and environmental change in cancer compared to normal tissue results in the measurable difference in fluorescence lifetime, making FLIM a sensitive surgical tool.

blocks.text: In contrast to fluorescence intensity measurements, fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) provides a robust metric for delineating tumour resection margin. ​ Fluorescence lifetime is the duration in which a fluorophore stays in its excited state before returning to the ground state. The fluorescence lifetime of a fluorophore is largely determined by the non-radiative decay rate, in other words, the restraint of molecular motion. For example, low temperature, high viscosity or a protein-bound state hinders non-radiative relaxation, thereby increases the fluorescence lifetime. Therefore, fluorescence lifetime is very sensitive to microenvironment and metabolic states. ​ ** Please check the Science for non-specialists page for the basics of FLIM ​ It has been demonstrated that FLIM enabled discrimination between glioblastoma and normal cortex with a high statistical significance ( p = 0.0027), more robust than intensity-based imaging ( p = 0.0199) (12).

blocks.html:
The robustness of FLIM is largely attributed to the fact that fluorescence lifetime is an intrinsic property, independent of NAD(P)H concentration and the detected intensity (15). Therefore, fluorescence lifetime remains uniform across the field of view, unaffected by background lighting.

​

Furthermore, fluorescence lifetime is influenced by various parameters that differentiate tumour from normal tissues. For example, the free and protein-bound states of NAD(P)H have distinct fluorescence lifetimes, and the free to bound ratio of NADH is linked to [NAD+]/[NADH] ratio (16, 17). In addition, the fluorescence lifetime of enzyme-bound NADH and NADPH are different and the lifetimes depend on enzyme binding configuration and which enzyme NAD(P)H is bound (18, 19). Therefore, the metabolic and environmental change in cancer compared to normal tissue results in the measurable difference in fluorescence lifetime, making FLIM a sensitive surgical tool.

blocks.html: What is fluorescence?

When a fluorescent molecule (fluorophore) absorbs a photon at a specific excitation wavelength, it transitions from ground state to excited states. The fluorophore may return to the ground state through radiative decay by emitting a photon with longer wavelength (fluorescence), or through non-radiative decay, which releases the energy without emitting a photon.

blocks.html: Tumour margin delineation with FLIM

In simplified terms, cancer cells reprogramme their glucose metabolism, leading to changes in cellular microenvironment and the composition of fluorescence molecules including NAD(P)H and FAD. Therefore, the fluorescence lifetimes of cancer and normal tissues are significantly different. This allows FLIM to delineate tumour margin, thereby guiding tumour resection in surgery.

posts.title: What Is Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging (FLIM)?
posts.html:
Fluorescence imaging is widely used in biological and biomedical research to visualise molecules, cells and tissues. While conventional fluorescence imaging often focuses on how bright a fluorescent signal is, another property of fluorescence can provide additional information: fluorescence lifetime.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) measures how long a fluorescent molecule remains in an excited state before returning to its ground state and emitting a photon. Rather than simply measuring fluorescence intensity, FLIM maps these fluorescence lifetimes across an image.

This provides a different way of examining biological tissue and can reveal information about the molecular environment that may not be apparent from fluorescence intensity alone.

How does fluorescence lifetime work?

When a fluorescent molecule absorbs light, it can be excited to a higher-energy state. The molecule remains in this excited state for a very short period before returning to its ground state, often releasing energy as fluorescence. The average time spent in the excited state is known as the fluorescence lifetime.

For many fluorophores, this occurs on the nanosecond timescale. Importantly, fluorescence lifetime can be influenced by the molecule's local environment and its interactions with other molecules.

FLIM measures these differences spatially, producing an image in which pixels contain fluorescence lifetime information rather than—or alongside—fluorescence intensity.

FLIM and cellular metabolism

One particularly interesting application of FLIM is the study of naturally fluorescent molecules involved in cellular metabolism. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NADH, and its phosphorylated counterpart NADPH are important metabolic cofactors. Their reduced forms are fluorescent and are often collectively described as NAD(P)H in fluorescence imaging. NAD(P)H can exist in different molecular environments, including free and protein-bound states. These states exhibit different fluorescence lifetimes. Consequently, FLIM measurements of NAD(P)H can provide information related to the metabolic state and molecular environment of cells and tissues. This makes fluorescence lifetime particularly interesting in cancer research, where tumour cells can exhibit metabolic and microenvironmental differences compared with surrounding normal tissue.

Why might FLIM be useful in cancer surgery?

A major challenge during cancer surgery is determining where tumour tissue ends and normal tissue begins. Tumour boundaries are not always clearly distinguishable by eye, and removing too little tissue may leave malignant cells behind. Conversely, removing excessive surrounding tissue may unnecessarily damage healthy structures and affect organ function.

Optical imaging technologies are therefore being investigated as potential ways of providing surgeons with additional information during an operation. Because FLIM can detect differences in fluorescence lifetime associated with tissue composition, metabolism and molecular environment, researchers are investigating whether these signals can help distinguish tumour tissue from surrounding normal tissue.

FLIM itself does not automatically identify cancer. The fluorescence lifetime data must be acquired, processed and interpreted appropriately before it can potentially contribute to surgical decision-making.

Where does artificial intelligence fit in?

FLIM datasets can contain large amounts of spatial and temporal information. Analysing these data rapidly is particularly important when considering potential intraoperative applications.

Artificial intelligence and machine-learning approaches can potentially assist by identifying patterns within imaging data and helping classify different tissue regions. This creates the possibility of combining FLIM with AI-assisted image analysis to transform complex fluorescence lifetime measurements into information that may be easier to interpret during surgery.

At SurgicGuide, this concept forms the basis of our AI-integrated FLIM System: a proposed approach combining fluorescence lifetime imaging with artificial intelligence for research into real-time tumour detection and precision cancer surgery.

FLIM versus fluorescence intensity imaging

Fluorescence intensity and fluorescence lifetime provide different types of information. Intensity imaging measures the amount of detected fluorescence and can be affected by factors such as fluorophore concentration, excitation intensity and detection conditions. FLIM instead measures the temporal behaviour of fluorescence following excitation.

This means lifetime measurements can provide information that complements conventional fluorescence intensity imaging. Neither approach is universally superior; the most appropriate measurement depends on the biological question and imaging application.

From FLIM research to surgical guidance

FLIM has been investigated across many areas of biomedical research, including cellular metabolism and cancer imaging. Translating these principles into practical intraoperative systems, however, introduces additional challenges.

A surgical imaging system needs to acquire useful information quickly, process complex data and present the result in a form that can potentially assist the surgeon without unnecessarily disrupting the surgical workflow. Combining fluorescence lifetime imaging, computational analysis and artificial intelligence is one potential approach to addressing these challenges.

For a more technical explanation of the underlying fluorescence science, visit our Specialist section. Further scientific literature supporting the principles discussed here can be found on our References page.

posts.title: Insights into the Biotech Industry: How to Build Your Network and Make Your CV Outstanding?
posts.html:
Hi everyone! I’m Valiant Cheung Ching-long, Chief Scientific Officer at SurgicGuide.

When I was starting out in science, I used to think that building a strong CV was mostly about getting good grades and gaining technical experience. Those things are definitely important, but over time, I’ve realised that your network and the experiences you gain from other people can be just as valuable.

So, how do you actually build your network?

For me, it starts with something very simple: talk to people. Go to seminars, conferences, career events, workshops, or even just have a conversation with someone whose work interests you. You don’t always need to be looking for a job or asking for something. Sometimes, a short conversation can lead to a new idea, a collaboration, or simply a different perspective.

When it comes to your CV, I think quality matters more than quantity. Instead of trying to list everything you have ever done, focus on experiences that show what you can actually contribute. Research projects, internships, technical skills, presentations, teamwork, leadership and problem-solving can all tell a story about you.

And don’t underestimate the value of showing what you’ve learned. Being able to explain your research clearly, discuss your technical skills, and talk about how an experience changed the way you think can make your CV much more meaningful than simply listing job titles.

Finally, networking isn’t about collecting as many contacts as possible. It’s about building genuine professional relationships over time.

The biotech industry is highly collaborative. You never know when a conversation, a research project, or a connection you make today might open the door to an opportunity tomorrow.

Keep learning, keep meeting people, and keep building your story.

— Valiant

Cheung, Ching-long

posts.title: Insights into the Biotech Industry: What is Regulatory Affairs?
posts.html:
Hi everyone! I’m Ben (Leung, Ho-bank), VP of Regulatory Affairs at SurgicGuide.

So, what exactly is regulatory affairs?

In the biotech and medical technology industry, regulatory affairs is essentially about connecting science and innovation with the regulatory requirements needed to bring a product to patients.

At SurgicGuide, my role involves thinking about questions such as: What regulatory pathway might our AI-integrated FLIM System follow? What evidence do we need to generate? What information needs to be included in a regulatory submission? And how do we make sure our development plans are aligned with regulatory expectations?

It’s not simply about preparing paperwork. Regulatory considerations can influence product development, clinical studies, risk management, quality systems, and market access from an early stage.

One of the most interesting parts of the job is working with different teams. I regularly communicate with scientists, engineers, clinicians, and product developers to make sure regulatory requirements are considered alongside the technology itself.

And because regulations differ between countries, regulatory affairs also has an international dimension. A product strategy that works in one market may need to be adapted for another.

For me, regulatory affairs is about helping innovative technologies make the journey from the laboratory to real-world use — responsibly and with the right evidence behind them.

— Ben

posts.title: Access to the Global Market: Beginning with the FDA
posts.html:
For SurgicGuide Limited, entering the global medical technology market begins with establishing a strong regulatory foundation. As one of the world's major medical-device markets, the United States provides an important starting point for demonstrating that the AI-integrated FLIM System can meet appropriate requirements for safety and effectiveness.

The FDA regulatory pathway depends on factors such as the device's intended use, risk profile, and technological characteristics. Potential pathways include 510(k) clearance, De Novo classification, and Premarket Approval (PMA). A 510(k) generally requires a legally marketed predicate device, while De Novo provides a pathway for certain novel low- to moderate-risk devices without a predicate. PMA is used for high-risk devices requiring the most rigorous premarket review.

For SurgicGuide, developing the AI-integrated FLIM System would therefore involve clearly defining its intended use and regulatory classification, establishing appropriate quality and risk-management systems, and generating the necessary non-clinical and clinical evidence to support an FDA submission. The appropriate regulatory pathway would ultimately depend on the specific characteristics and intended use of the system.

Achieving U.S. market authorization would represent an important regulatory milestone, but it would not automatically authorize marketing in other countries. Medical-device requirements vary between jurisdictions, requiring SurgicGuide to develop additional regulatory strategies for other major markets.

International initiatives such as the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) aim to promote greater harmonisation and convergence of medical-device regulatory requirements. SurgicGuide could therefore use its U.S. regulatory experience as part of a broader strategy for international expansion, while addressing the specific requirements of each target market.
